{{Short description|Polynomial whose coefficients are all 1 or −1}}
{{About|polynomials with coefficients 1 or −1|the conjecture in Diophantine approximation|Littlewood conjecture|the symmetric functions|Hall–Littlewood polynomials}}

[[File:Roots_of_all_16th_degree_Littlewood_polynomials.png|thumb|upright=1.15|alt=Plot of the complex roots of every Littlewood polynomial of degree 16|Roots of all Littlewood polynomials of degree 16.]]
[[File:LittlewoodPolynomialRootsDegree1-14.gif|thumb|upright=1.15|alt=Animation plotting the complex roots of Littlewood polynomials degree by degree from 1 through 14|Roots of all Littlewood polynomials of degrees 1 through 14.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''Littlewood polynomial''' is a polynomial whose coefficients are all either <math>1</math> or <math>-1</math>. Equivalently, its coefficient vector is a finite binary sign sequence. Littlewood polynomials are named after [[J. E. Littlewood]], who studied their values on the [[unit circle]] and posed several influential extremal problems about them in the 1960s.<ref name="Littlewood1966">{{cite journal |last=Littlewood |first=J. E. |title=On polynomials <math>\sum \pm z^m</math>, <math>\sum e^{\alpha_m i}z^m</math>, <math>z=e^{i\theta}</math> |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |series=1 |volume=41 |year=1966 |pages=367–376 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-41.1.367 }}</ref><ref name="Littlewood1968">{{cite book |last=Littlewood |first=J. E. |title=Some Problems in Real and Complex Analysis |series=Heath Mathematical Monographs |publisher=D. C. Heath |location=Lexington, Massachusetts |year=1968 }}</ref>

The natural size of a Littlewood polynomial of degree <math>n</math> on the unit circle is <math>\sqrt{n+1}</math>, because its normalized <math>L^2</math> norm is exactly that value. A central question asked whether the modulus could remain between two fixed positive multiples of <math>\sqrt{n+1}</math> at every point of the circle. Littlewood conjectured that this was possible; the conjecture was proved in 2020 by Paul Balister, [[Béla Bollobás]], [[Robert Morris (mathematician)|Robert Morris]], [[Julian Sahasrabudhe]], and Marius Tiba.<ref name="Balister2020">{{cite journal |last1=Balister |first1=Paul |last2=Bollobás |first2=Béla |last3=Morris |first3=Robert |last4=Sahasrabudhe |first4=Julian |last5=Tiba |first5=Marius |title=Flat Littlewood polynomials exist |journal=Annals of Mathematics |series=2 |volume=192 |issue=3 |year=2020 |pages=977–1004 |doi=10.4007/annals.2020.192.3.6 |arxiv=1907.09464 }}</ref> Stronger questions about asymptotically constant modulus, extremal <math>L^q</math> norms, [[Mahler measure]], zero distribution, and autocorrelation remain active.

== Definition and elementary properties ==
A polynomial
<math display="block">
P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n} a_jz^j
</math>
is a Littlewood polynomial of degree <math>n</math> if <math>a_j\in\{-1,1\}</math> for every <math>j</math>. There are <math>2^{n+1}</math> such polynomials. Multiplication by <math>-1</math>, the substitution <math>z\mapsto -z</math>, and passage to the reciprocal polynomial
<math display="block">
P^*(z)=z^nP(1/z)
</math>
preserve the class. These operations account for many of the natural symmetries used in enumerations.

Every zero <math>\alpha</math> of a Littlewood polynomial satisfies
<math display="block">
\frac12<|\alpha|<2.
</math>
Indeed, when <math>|z|\leq 1/2</math>, the constant term has greater modulus than the sum of all remaining terms, and the upper bound follows by applying the same argument to the reciprocal polynomial.

For <math>0<q<\infty</math>, its normalized norm on the unit circle is
<math display="block">
\lVert P\rVert_q=
\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|P(e^{it})|^q\,dt\right)^{1/q},
</math>
and <math>\lVert P\rVert_\infty=\max_{|z|=1}|P(z)|</math>. Parseval's identity gives
<math display="block">
\lVert P\rVert_2^2=\sum_{j=0}^{n}|a_j|^2=n+1.
</math>
Thus <math>\sqrt{n+1}</math> is the root-mean-square modulus and the reference scale in flatness problems.

== Flatness on the unit circle ==
A sequence of Littlewood polynomials <math>(P_n)</math>, with <math>\deg P_n=n</math>, is called '''flat''' if there are absolute constants <math>0<c<C</math> such that
<math display="block">
c\sqrt{n+1}\leq |P_n(z)|\leq C\sqrt{n+1}
\qquad (|z|=1)
</math>
for every <math>n</math> in the sequence. The upper and lower bounds play different roles: the upper bound limits peaks, while the lower bound excludes zeros and deep troughs on the unit circle.

=== Rudin–Shapiro polynomials ===
The [[Shapiro polynomials|Rudin–Shapiro polynomials]] provide a classical explicit upper-bound construction. Define
<math display="block">
P_0(z)=Q_0(z)=1,
</math>
and recursively
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
P_{m+1}(z)&=P_m(z)+z^{2^m}Q_m(z),\\
Q_{m+1}(z)&=P_m(z)-z^{2^m}Q_m(z).
\end{aligned}
</math>
Both <math>P_m</math> and <math>Q_m</math> are Littlewood polynomials with <math>N=2^m</math> coefficients. On the unit circle they satisfy
<math display="block">
|P_m(z)|^2+|Q_m(z)|^2=2N,
</math>
and hence <math>\lVert P_m\rVert_\infty,\lVert Q_m\rVert_\infty\leq\sqrt{2N}</math>.<ref name="Rudin1959">{{cite journal |last=Rudin |first=Walter |authorlink=Walter Rudin |title=Some theorems on Fourier coefficients |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=10 |year=1959 |pages=855–859 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1959-0116184-5 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This does not by itself give a uniform positive lower bound. Rodgers proved in 2017 that suitably normalized values of the Rudin–Shapiro polynomials become uniformly distributed in the unit disk.<ref name="Rodgers2017">{{cite journal |last=Rodgers |first=Brad |title=On the distribution of Rudin–Shapiro polynomials and lacunary walks on <math>SU(2)</math> |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |volume=320 |year=2017 |pages=993–1008 |doi=10.1016/j.aim.2017.09.022 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1606.01637 }}</ref> In 2026, Erdélyi quantified their oscillation around the middle of their range, proving upper and lower bounds for the number of solutions of <math>|P_m(e^{it})|^2=N</math> and <math>|Q_m(e^{it})|^2=N</math> on every subarc of the unit circle.<ref name="Erdelyi2026Oscillation">{{cite journal |last=Erdélyi |first=Tamás |title=On the Oscillation of the Modulus of the Rudin–Shapiro Polynomials Around the Middle of Their Ranges |journal=Computational Methods and Function Theory |year=2026 |doi=10.1007/s40315-026-00620-y |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Littlewood's flatness conjecture ===
Littlewood conjectured in 1966 that flat Littlewood polynomials exist. An influential earlier contribution was József Beck's 1991 paper on flat polynomials and Littlewood's problem.<ref name="Beck1991">{{cite journal |last=Beck |first=József |title=Flat Polynomials on the Unit Circle—Note on a Problem of Littlewood |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=23 |issue=3 |year=1991 |pages=269–277 |doi=10.1112/blms/23.3.269 }}</ref> Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba proved the stronger statement that there are absolute constants <math>\Delta>\delta>0</math> such that, for every <math>n\geq2</math>, some Littlewood polynomial <math>P</math> of degree <math>n</math> satisfies
<math display="block">
\delta\sqrt n\leq |P(z)|\leq\Delta\sqrt n
\qquad (|z|=1).
</math>
Their proof combines discrepancy theory with probabilistic and combinatorial methods.<ref name="Balister2020" /> It resolved Littlewood's 1966 conjecture after more than five decades.

=== Ultraflat polynomials ===
A sequence is '''ultraflat''' if
<math display="block">
\max_{|z|=1}
\left|\frac{|P_n(z)|}{\sqrt{n+1}}-1\right|\longrightarrow0.
</math>
Jean-Pierre Kahane proved that ultraflat sequences exist when the coefficients are allowed to be arbitrary complex numbers of modulus <math>1</math>.<ref name="Kahane1980">{{cite journal |last=Kahane |first=Jean-Pierre |title=Sur les polynômes à coefficients unimodulaires |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=12 |issue=5 |year=1980 |pages=321–342 |doi=10.1112/blms/12.5.321 }}</ref> Bombieri and Bourgain later obtained stronger quantitative constructions in this unimodular setting.<ref name="BombieriBourgain2009">{{cite journal |last1=Bombieri |first1=Enrico |authorlink1=Enrico Bombieri |last2=Bourgain |first2=Jean |authorlink2=Jean Bourgain |title=On Kahane's ultraflat polynomials |journal=[[Journal of the European Mathematical Society]] |volume=11 |issue=3 |year=2009 |pages=627–703 |doi=10.4171/JEMS/163 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Erdős conjectured that no ultraflat Littlewood sequence exists. The general <math>\{-1,1\}</math> problem remains open in the peer-reviewed literature; bounded flatness, proved in 2020, is substantially weaker than ultraflatness.<ref name="BorweinMossinghoff2008">{{cite book |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Mossinghoff |first2=Michael J. |chapter=Barker sequences and flat polynomials |title=Number Theory and Polynomials |series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series |volume=352 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2008 |pages=71–88 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511721274.007 }}</ref><ref name="Steinerberger2024">{{cite journal |last=Steinerberger |first=Stefan |title=A note on approximate Hadamard matrices |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=92 |year=2024 |pages=3125–3131 |doi=10.1007/s10623-024-01430-w }}</ref>

== Autocorrelation, <math>L^4</math> norm, and merit factor ==
Let <math>P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a_jz^j</math>, and define the nontrivial '''aperiodic autocorrelations'''
<math display="block">
C(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1-k}a_ja_{j+k}
\qquad (1\leq k<N).
</math>
Expanding the squared modulus gives
<math display="block">
|P(e^{it})|^2=N+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}C(k)\cos(kt),
</math>
and Parseval then yields the exact identity
<math display="block">
\lVert P\rVert_4^4=N^2+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}C(k)^2.
</math>
Consequently, minimizing the <math>L^4</math> norm is equivalent to minimizing the total squared aperiodic autocorrelation.

The associated '''merit factor''' is
<math display="block">
F(P)=\frac{N^2}{2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}C(k)^2}
     =\frac{N^2}{\lVert P\rVert_4^4-N^2}.
</math>
High merit factor means that the coefficient sequence has low aggregate autocorrelation. This problem originated in communications and signal design and has generated a large literature on character sequences, difference sets, and recursive constructions.<ref name="Golay1983">{{cite journal |last=Golay |first=Marcel J. E. |title=The merit factor of Legendre sequences |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=29 |issue=6 |year=1983 |pages=934–936 |doi=10.1109/TIT.1983.1056744 }}</ref><ref name="JedwabKatzSchmidt2013">{{cite journal |last1=Jedwab |first1=Jonathan |last2=Katz |first2=Daniel J. |last3=Schmidt |first3=Kai-Uwe |title=Advances in the merit factor problem for binary sequences |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series A |volume=120 |issue=4 |year=2013 |pages=882–906 |doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2013.01.010 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

A [[Barker code|Barker sequence]] is a sign sequence satisfying <math>|C(k)|\leq1</math> for every nonzero shift. Such sequences therefore produce exceptionally small <math>L^4</math> defect. Barker sequences are known only for lengths <math>1,2,3,4,5,7,11,13</math>; no odd Barker sequence has length greater than <math>13</math>, while the existence of a longer even one remains open.<ref name="SchmidtSurvey2016">{{cite journal |last=Schmidt |first=Kai-Uwe |title=Sequences with small correlation |journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography |volume=78 |issue=1 |year=2016 |pages=237–267 |doi=10.1007/s10623-015-0154-7 }}</ref>

Arithmetic constructions also provide tractable norm problems. For an odd prime <math>p</math>, the Fekete polynomial
<math display="block">
f_p(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\left(\frac{j}{p}\right)z^j
</math>
is defined using the [[Legendre symbol]]; <math>z^{-1}f_p(z)</math> is a Littlewood polynomial. Explicit limiting formulas are known for its normalized even <math>L^q</math> norms and for related finite-field character polynomials.<ref name="GuntherSchmidt2017">{{cite journal |last1=Günther |first1=Christian |last2=Schmidt |first2=Kai-Uwe |title=<math>L^q</math> norms of Fekete and related polynomials |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |volume=69 |issue=4 |year=2017 |pages=807–825 |doi=10.4153/CJM-2016-023-4 }}</ref>

== Mahler measure ==
The [[Mahler measure]] of a nonzero polynomial is the [[geometric mean]] of its modulus on the unit circle,
<math display="block">
M(P)=\exp\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|P(e^{it})|\,dt\right).
</math>
It satisfies <math>M(P)\leq\lVert P\rVert_2=\sqrt N</math> for a Littlewood polynomial with <math>N</math> coefficients. Flat Littlewood polynomials have Mahler measure comparable to <math>\sqrt N</math> because their modulus has a uniform lower bound of that order.

For the Rudin–Shapiro polynomials, Erdélyi first proved a lower bound of order <math>\sqrt N</math><ref name="Erdelyi2016">{{cite journal |last=Erdélyi |first=Tamás |title=The Mahler measure of the Rudin–Shapiro polynomials |journal=Constructive Approximation |volume=43 |issue=3 |year=2016 |pages=357–369 |doi=10.1007/s00365-015-9297-z }}</ref> and later proved Saffari's conjectured asymptotic
<math display="block">
M(P_m)\sim M(Q_m)\sim\sqrt{\frac{2N}{e}}
\qquad (N=2^m).
</math>
<ref name="Erdelyi2020Mahler">{{cite journal |last=Erdélyi |first=Tamás |title=The asymptotic value of the Mahler measure of the Rudin–Shapiro polynomials |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |volume=142 |issue=2 |year=2020 |pages=521–537 |doi=10.1007/s11854-020-0142-3 |arxiv=1708.01189 }}</ref> Mahler measure also links Littlewood polynomials to algebraic-number-theoretic questions about reciprocal polynomials and small algebraic integers. For example, Borwein, Hare, and Mossinghoff determined the minimum Mahler measure of a nonreciprocal polynomial with all coefficients odd and computed the smallest measures of reciprocal Littlewood polynomials through degree <math>72</math>.<ref name="BorweinHareMossinghoff2004">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Hare |first2=Kevin G. |last3=Mossinghoff |first3=Michael J. |title=The Mahler measure of polynomials with odd coefficients |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=36 |issue=3 |year=2004 |pages=332–338 |doi=10.1112/S002460930300287X }}</ref>

== Zeros ==
The distribution of zeros of Littlewood polynomials is highly varied despite the elementary coefficient restriction. Some polynomials have roots on the unit circle, while others have none. For degrees <math>n</math> with <math>n+1</math> prime, Borwein, Choi, Ferguson, and Jankauskas proved that for every <math>0\leq k\leq n-1</math> there is a degree-<math>n</math> Littlewood polynomial with exactly <math>k</math> zeros in the open unit disk and no zeros on its boundary.<ref name="BorweinChoiFergusonJankauskas2015">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Choi |first2=Stephen |last3=Ferguson |first3=Ron |last4=Jankauskas |first4=Jonas |title=On Littlewood polynomials with prescribed number of zeros inside the unit disk |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |volume=67 |issue=3 |year=2015 |pages=507–526 |doi=10.4153/CJM-2014-007-1 }}</ref>

A '''random Littlewood polynomial''' has independent coefficients taking the values <math>1</math> and <math>-1</math> with equal probability. This model goes back to work of Littlewood and Offord on random algebraic equations.<ref name="LittlewoodOfford1938">{{cite journal |last1=Littlewood |first1=J. E. |last2=Offord |first2=A. C. |title=On the number of real roots of a random algebraic equation |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |series=1 |volume=13 |issue=4 |year=1938 |pages=288–295 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-13.4.288 }}</ref> Yakir proved that, as <math>N\to\infty</math>, all but <math>o(2^N)</math> Littlewood polynomials with <math>N</math> coefficients have <math>N/2+o(N)</math> zeros inside the unit disk.<ref name="Yakir2021">{{cite journal |last=Yakir |first=Oren |title=Approximately half of the roots of a random Littlewood polynomial are inside the disk |journal=Studia Mathematica |volume=261 |issue=2 |year=2021 |pages=227–240 |doi=10.4064/sm201117-28-1 |arxiv=2011.06234 }}</ref> For the same Rademacher coefficient model, Do, Nguyen, and Vu proved that the expected number of real roots of a degree-<math>n</math> polynomial is
<math display="block">
\frac{2}{\pi}\log n+C+o(1),
</math>
where <math>C</math> is a constant depending on the coefficient distribution.<ref name="DoNguyenVu2015">{{cite journal |last1=Do |first1=Yen |last2=Nguyen |first2=Hoi |last3=Vu |first3=Van |title=Real roots of random polynomials: expectation and repulsion |journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society |series=3 |volume=111 |issue=6 |year=2015 |pages=1231–1260 |doi=10.1112/plms/pdv055 |arxiv=1409.4128 }}</ref>

Random coefficients also have a predictable norm profile. Borwein and Lockhart obtained asymptotic expected <math>L^q</math> norms for broad classes of independent coefficients,<ref name="BorweinLockhart2001">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Lockhart |first2=Richard |title=The expected <math>L_p</math> norm of random polynomials |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=129 |issue=5 |year=2001 |pages=1463–1472 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-00-05690-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and Duan, Fang, and Zhan proved in 2024 that for random Littlewood polynomials <math>P_N</math> with <math>N</math> coefficients,
<math display="block">
\frac{\lVert P_N\rVert_4}{\sqrt N}\longrightarrow 2^{1/4}
</math>
almost surely.<ref name="DuanFangZhan2024">{{cite journal |last1=Duan |first1=Yongjiang |last2=Fang |first2=Xiang |last3=Zhan |first3=Na |title=Almost sure convergence of the <math>L^4</math> norm of Littlewood polynomials |journal=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin |volume=67 |issue=3 |year=2024 |pages=872–885 |doi=10.4153/S0008439524000213 }}</ref>

== Arithmetic and algebraic questions ==
Littlewood polynomials also give rise to Diophantine and Galois-theoretic problems. Hajdu, Herendi, Tengely, and Varga studied when a Littlewood polynomial takes a square value at an integer argument. They classified the square values for degrees <math>3</math> and <math>5</math> and for every even degree at most <math>24</math>, and gave computational data for odd degrees at most <math>17</math>.<ref name="HajduEtAl2024">{{cite journal |last1=Hajdu |first1=Lajos |last2=Herendi |first2=Orsolya |last3=Tengely |first3=Szabolcs |last4=Varga |first4=Nóra |title=Square values of Littlewood polynomials |journal=The Ramanujan Journal |volume=65 |year=2024 |pages=1205–1226 |doi=10.1007/s11139-024-00935-1 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

For random Littlewood polynomials, it is conjectured that the probability of irreducibility tends to <math>1</math> with the degree. In 2025, Bary-Soroker, Hokken, Kozma, and Poonen proved unconditionally that
<math display="block">
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr(P_n\text{ is irreducible})=1.
</math>
More precisely, there is a constant <math>c>0</math> such that, when <math>n=p^r-1</math>, with <math>p=2</math> or with <math>p\geq7</math> a prime for which <math>2</math> generates <math>(\mathbb Z/p^2\mathbb Z)^\times</math>, a random degree-<math>n</math> Littlewood polynomial is irreducible with probability at least <math>1-n^{-c}</math>.<ref name="BarySorokerEtAl2025">{{cite journal |last1=Bary-Soroker |first1=Lior |last2=Hokken |first2=David |last3=Kozma |first3=Gady |last4=Poonen |first4=Bjorn |title=Irreducibility of Littlewood Polynomials of Special Degrees |journal=International Mathematics Research Notices |volume=2025 |issue=21 |year=2025 |at=rnaf326 |doi=10.1093/imrn/rnaf326 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

For reciprocal and skew-reciprocal Littlewood polynomials, Hokken obtained leading-term asymptotics for the number having square discriminant. The result is related to a bounded-height analogue of a conjecture of van der Waerden on [[Galois group]]s of random polynomials.<ref name="Hokken2026">{{cite journal |last=Hokken |first=David |title=Counting (skew-)reciprocal Littlewood polynomials with square discriminant |journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]] |year=2026 |doi=10.1007/s11856-026-2909-4 |arxiv=2301.05656 }}</ref>

== Values at roots of unity ==
For a Littlewood polynomial with <math>N</math> coefficients, define the periodic autocorrelations
<math display="block">
R(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a_ja_{j+t\bmod N}.
</math>
If <math>\omega=e^{2\pi i/N}</math>, the discrete Fourier transform gives
<math display="block">
|P(\omega^k)|^2=\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}R(t)\omega^{kt}.
</math>
Therefore
<math display="block">
|P(\omega^k)|=\sqrt N\quad(0\leq k<N)
</math>
if and only if <math>R(0)=N</math> and every nontrivial periodic autocorrelation is zero. The circulant matrix whose first row is <math>(a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1})</math> is then a [[circulant Hadamard matrix]].

[[Ryser's conjecture on circulant Hadamard matrices]] states that this exact discrete flatness occurs only for <math>N=1</math> and <math>N=4</math>. The required modulus is therefore <math>\sqrt N</math>. A quantitative strengthening proposed by Steinerberger asks whether there is an absolute <math>\varepsilon_0>0</math> such that every Littlewood polynomial of length <math>N>4</math> satisfies
<math display="block">
\max_{0\leq k<N}\left||P(\omega^k)|-\sqrt N\right|
\geq\varepsilon_0N^{1/4}.
</math>
<ref name="Steinerberger2024" />

== Related coefficient classes ==
Several nearby families are studied with similar methods. '''Newman polynomials''' have coefficients in <math>\{0,1\}</math>, while '''Borwein polynomials''' have coefficients in <math>\{-1,0,1\}</math>. '''Unimodular polynomials''' allow arbitrary complex coefficients of absolute value <math>1</math>; Kahane's ultraflat construction belongs to this larger class. [[Fekete polynomial]]s are character polynomials with coefficients given by Legendre symbols, and after removal of their zero constant coefficient they give Littlewood polynomials. Cyclotomic Littlewood polynomials, whose roots are all roots of unity, form another structured subclass with explicitly computable norms.<ref name="BorweinChoiFerguson2005">{{cite journal |last1=Borwein |first1=Peter |last2=Choi |first2=Kwok-Kwong Stephen |last3=Ferguson |first3=Ron |title=Norms of cyclotomic Littlewood polynomials |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=138 |issue=2 |year=2005 |pages=315–326 |doi=10.1017/S0305004104008199 }}</ref>

== Open problems ==
The 2020 flatness theorem settles the existence of uniformly bounded upper and lower constants, but does not determine optimal constants or produce ultraflat Littlewood polynomials. The existence or nonexistence of an ultraflat Littlewood sequence remains a central open question. Other major problems include determining the optimal asymptotic merit factor, or equivalently the smallest possible normalized <math>L^4</math> norm; deciding whether Barker sequences of length greater than <math>13</math> exist; resolving Ryser's conjecture on exact flatness at roots of unity; and proving that a random Littlewood polynomial is irreducible with probability tending to <math>1</math> without restricting the degree to special subsequences.<ref name="SchmidtSurvey2016" /><ref name="Steinerberger2024" /><ref name="BarySorokerEtAl2025" />
